reason: I’ll join the bones to start the arm’s framework for the joint.
expectation: I expect an arm framework, though it may still need cartilage and ligaments to form a working joint.

alternatives.reason: Cartilage and joint fluid also seem useful for a smooth joint, but I want to assemble the bones first.

effect: The bones provide rigid supports, but they still need a joint where they can turn relative to each other.
reaction: The distinction between bending bones and movement at a joint is clear.
reason: I’ll combine cartilage and joint fluid to prepare the smooth joint surfaces; it’s the only available combination.
expectation: I expect a smooth or lubricated joint surface that can later be fitted to the arm bones.

effect: The cartilage covers bone ends and joint fluid helps them slide; the next goal is to join the framework and attach the muscles.
reaction: The explanation makes the purpose of both joint components clear.
reason: I’ll fit the smooth surfaces to the arm bones to start joining the framework; it’s the only available combination.
expectation: I expect an arm framework with smooth surfaces at the joint, though it may still need ligaments and muscles.

effect: The joint surfaces allow the forearm to turn, but the articulated bones still need a pulling force.
reaction: The distinction between allowing movement and producing it is useful.
reason: I’ll add ligaments to the articulated bones; it’s the only available combination and should help hold the joint together.
expectation: I expect a more stable joint that will still need the muscles attached.

effect: The ligaments connect the bones and stabilize the joint; the framework now has slots for both opposing pulls.
reaction: The distinction between ligaments and the muscle tendons is useful.
reason: I’ll attach the bending muscles to fill one of the framework’s pull slots.
expectation: I expect the bending muscles to fit the front pull slot, leaving the rear pull to attach.

alternatives.reason: The straightening muscles should also fit, but either pull seems reasonable to attach first.

effect: The front muscles pull through tendons to bend the elbow, and relaxing them does not push the bones back. The opposing muscles still need to be attached.
reaction: The explanation of why an opposing pull is needed is useful.
reason: I’ll attach the straightening muscles to complete the opposing pulls; it’s the only available combination.
expectation: I expect the straightening muscles to fit the rear pull slot, completing the muscle attachments.

effect: The opposing muscles complete the framework: their pulls can bend, straighten and steady the elbow, including while holding a weight still. Coordination remains a separate job.
reaction: Holding a weight still without the muscles shortening was a useful addition to the picture of how they work.

mostWorthwhile.text: Attaching the bending muscles was most worthwhile because the result explained how tendons transmit a pull and why relaxing a muscle does not push the bones back.

leastWorthwhile.text: Joining the smooth surfaces to the bones felt least engaging as a decision: it was the only combination offered and its result was fairly predictable, though the explanation was useful.

surprise.text: The completed framework showed that muscles can keep pulling without shortening, such as when holding a weight still.

arbitrary.text: No action felt without purpose. The order of attaching the two muscle groups seemed interchangeable, so choosing the bending muscles first was a preference rather than a meaningful discovery.

continue.text: I would probably continue to see how the opposing muscles are coordinated. The links between joint structure and muscle pulls were clear, although several choices were predictable.
